In this video, I'll show you Traycer, a free and open-source desktop app for macOS, Linux and Windows that gives your coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Cursor one workspace, and that just launched mobile apps for iOS and Android. First, I'll show you how to make your own theme with Create Theme and Import Theme, including bringing over a VS Code theme. Then I'll set up a remote host so the repo, agents, terminals and credentials stay on one machine while you operate the same workspace from another desktop or your phone. After that, I'll use the new mobile app to start a task, answer the agent's question, approve a permission and get notifications, and then cover the in-app browser that both you and your agents can use. items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] Hi, welcome to another video. So today I want to talk about Tracer. Tracer is a free and open-source desktop app for Mac OS, Linux, and Windows. It gives your coding agents one workspace where they can work together and you direct the work from there. And they just launched mobile apps for Android and iOS. So you can now continue the same work from your phone while the agents keep running on your computer. We'll get to that in a bit. First, a quick look at what Tracer is. You bring your own subscriptions so you can run clawed code, codec, open code, cursor, and other coding agents side by side. Tracer doesn't make you buy another plan to use them, which I like a lot. The agents can also talk to each other. One agent can ask another one a question, ask for a review, or hand its work to the next agent. You don't have to copy messages from one chat to the other. Everything lives inside a task. A task holds its files, artifacts, history, and working context. So, you can switch models in the middle of a chat and you don't lose the thread, which is super useful when one model gets stuck and you want a second opinion. There are also built-in skills. These are reusable workflows for planning, debugging, reviewing, and writing docs. And you get multiplayer workspaces so your teammates can open your tasks and comment on artifacts in the same shared space. A task also brings your chats, files, artifacts, git diffs, pull requests, terminals, and browsers into panels. You can keep these panels open side by side so you see the chat and the result at the same time. Now, here's what I'll show you today. First, how to customize the workspace with your own theme. Then, how to use a remote host so you can operate the same workspace from another machine. After that, the new mobile apps where you keep the work moving from your phone. Then, the in-app browser, which you and your agents both use, and then model routing, which keeps a chat alive when a provider hits a rate limit. At the end, I'll also tell you about what Tracer is building next, which is long running automations. So, let's get right into it. If you're wondering how I got this theme, here's how to do it. Open settings, then go to appearance. Here you have two options. The first option is create theme. This makes a copy of the theme you use now, and you edit that copy. You change the colors here, and the preview updates live, so you see the result right away. When you like it, click save theme. The second option is import theme. Here you can browse community themes or you can import a tracer theme file or a VS Code theme file. So if you already have a VS Code theme that you love, you can just bring it over once the theme is saved. You can set it as your light theme or your dark theme. You can also stay with the built-in themes or let Tracer follow your device appearance. So it switches between light and dark on its own. And if you make a theme you're proud of, you can export it and share it with other people. So that's great. Now let's talk about the remote host. Tracer lets you use your laptop, desktop, dev box or VM as a remote host. Then you connect from another desktop or from your phone and you operate the same workspace. The idea is simple. The host holds the repo. The running agents, the terminals, the browser sessions and your credentials. The code and the execution stay on the host. Nothing gets copied to your phone. Your phone or your second machine is just a window into the host. To set it up, you register the host first. Then you connect from another device and you continue the same tasks, chats, artifacts, terminals, and browsers right where you left them. Access is tied to your Tracer account. And you can manage your registered hosts and devices or remove them when you don't need them anymore. So if you lose a device, you can just remove it. And the best example of this is the phone. So let's look at the mobile app. The Tracer app is on both Android and iOS. The links for the App Store and the Play Store are in the description. You sign in and you pick up the same workspace on your phone. The agents keep running on the host. And this is not just a status dashboard where you watch things happen. You can actually start work from here and give the agents the input they need. So, let me start a task from the phone. I'll type what I want. And I can attach an image, too, if that helps the agent understand. Let's send it. Now, the agent has a question for me. I can answer it right here. And here, it asks for a permission, so I'll approve it. If I want to change the direction, I can send a follow-up instruction the same way I do on the desktop. You also get notifications. When an agent needs you, or when it finishes, your phone tells you. You tap the notification and it opens that task directly. So you don't need to sit in front of your laptop and wait for an agent to finish which is just amazing to be honest. On the phone the panels open full screen and you switch between them. So you can check the files, the artifacts, the git diffs and the pull requests. You can also open the terminals and even the browser which the host streams to your phone. The terminal also has an onscreen key bar. It gives you keys like escape, tab, control, and the arrow keys. A phone keyboard doesn't have those keys. So, this makes the terminal actually usable on a phone. Now, a few things to keep in mind. You need an active remote host for this to work because the agents don't run on the phone. The phone also can't act as a host and it can't restart a host. And voice dictation isn't available in the mobile app yet. But for keeping your work moving while you're away from your desk, this is really good stuff. Now, let's come to the inapp browser. Tracer has a browser panel inside the task right next to your chats, terminals, and files. And both you and your agents can operate it. When you open the browser, its start page shows the local dev servers that it detects. So if your app is running, you just click it and it opens. Now, let's say something on the page looks wrong. Instead of describing it in a long message, you select the exact component, annotate it, and send that crop to the agent as chat context. So the agent knows exactly which part you mean. This saves a lot of back and forth. The agent can also use this browser to verify its own work. It navigates the page, inspects it, clicks elements and takes screenshots to check that the change works. And if it reaches a login page, a capture, or an MFA prompt, it hands control back to you. You finish that step, and the agent continues. You can also pop the browser out into a floating picturein picture window, so your app stays visible while you work in other panels. I think that's super cool. One small note, the local browser has dev tools, viewport presets, and annotation. When the browser streams from a remote host to another desktop, you get the navigation and the address bar, but not those local only tools. Now, let's talk about model routing. We all know the pain. You're in the middle of a chat and the provider hits a rate limit or goes down. Model routing keeps the chat moving when that happens. Open settings, then go to model routing. Here you build a fallback plan. The plan can try another account on the same provider or it can switch to an equivalent model on another provider. It can also wait for your usage limit to reset. And if no fallback works, it notifies you. You choose the order of these steps. You also choose which models can replace one another. If a switch is pending and you don't want it, you can cancel it. And you decide whether the chat switches back to the original provider when that provider is available again. A few details here. Automatic routing is off by default, so you need to turn it on. It applies to chat agents on the selected host, not to terminal agents. When it switches, it starts a new agent session that uses the chat history. So the new model has the context and the wait option only works when the provider gives a reset time and that time is within the maximum weight you set. If you have multiple subscriptions like me, this is quite great to see. Now before I end this video, let's talk about what Tracer is working toward, and that's longunning automations. The idea is agents and automations that handle ongoing work without you watching them all the time. They come back to you only when your input matters. Think of the automations as Grubbots, but for engineering. The vision also includes direct monitoring of your logging, analytics, and observability tools like Sentry, Post Hog, and Data Dog. So, the automations keep an eye on what's happening, and you don't have to check those tools all day. The workflows are meant to be self-improving. The automations review their own performance on a regular basis, and they improve the workflow over time. They're always on, and you can reach them from anywhere. You get laptop and mobile access and the work runs in the cloud. So the work isn't tied to a laptop that has to stay open. There's also less noise. You get involved only when an important decision, an approval or some other input needs you. They also want the automations to make proactive suggestions. So they look at your existing workflows and your codebase and they find more things that you can automate. It's provider agnostic too. You use models across providers and bring your own subscriptions. Same as the desktop app. Your keys are managed centrally and securely for automation use. You can share automations with your team with user group access controls and environments and they provide sandboxes where the automation work runs. Now, this part isn't out yet. It's the vision, but if you're interested in trying this out, join the wait list using the link in the description. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me [music] know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll [music] see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

items.title: Hydrogen by Google is KINDA GOOD...
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

PandaCode: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode

In this video, I'll review Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Google's fast, cheap model for everyday coding and agentic work, starting with its positioning, pricing, speed, and availability. I'll put it through the six KingBench 4 app builds and show what actually works, what breaks, and how it compares with Carbon, Argon, and the competition. Then I'll look at its cost and behavior, including the tests that pass while the app is still broken. I'll explain how I would use it as a worker under a stronger lead in PandaCode, my app for running coding agents as a team, and how that compares with Google's Antigravity Orchestrator. Finally, I'll give my take on whether Google is behind in the AI race and why Hydrogen needs an independent reviewer before you trust its finished work.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Gemini 4 Hydrogen is adapted from Carbon and built for quick e
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So Google has launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It came out on November 12th about two weeks after Carbon and it is the fast cheap model of the Gemini 4 family. I ran it on all six King Bench 4 apps and the results surprised me. Today I'll cover what it is, what it built, how it works, and whether Google is now behind in the AI race. First, the basics. Google says Hydrogen is adapted from Carbon. Carbon and Argon are the deep reasoning models for long hard problems and Hydrogen is built for quick execution in agentic work. It replaces Gemini 3.8 Flash. Google never says the Flash name is gone, but there is no Gemini 4 Flash and Hydrogen is the model they tell you to move to. The price is $1.50 per million output tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens flat across the whole 1 million token context window. That is double what 3.8 Flash costs today, but 3.8 Flash goes up to the same price on January 1. Carbon and Argon are 220 and 220 Argon until the end of November and $4 and $20 after that. So from December, Hydrogen is 62.5% cheaper than both. It also has a free tier in the API which Carbon and Argon do not. Google says it finishes tasks 2.5 times faster than 3.8 Flash. Artificial analysis measured 8.3 minutes per task against 14.7 for 3.8 Flash which is about 1.8 times. So it is fast, just not as fast as the claim on their intelligence index. Hydrogen at high effort scores 51, 1 point above Argon and 54 at the new X high level. Carbon is at 60 and Fable 5.2 at max effort is at 65. It is also everywhere on day one, AI Studio and the API, the Gemini app, Anti-Gravity where it is now the default Asian model and Google Search for all users. Now the benchmark. King Bench 4 is six apps, one prompt each, no follow-ups and independent evaluators score each app out of 10 with a rubric. I ran Hydrogen and OpenCode 2.2.7 at high effort on the same route and settings as Carbon. Carbon ran on an older OpenCode version, so keep that in mind when I compare the two. The first app is the emulator and it scored 3.2. The GameBoy port is genuinely good. It passes Blargg's CPU and timing tests and both Acid2 rendering tests are pixel exact. The DS and 3DS cores are real interpreters, not just header parsers, but they barely run. 15 of 16 DS homebrew ROMs and all 11 3DS homebrew stay on a blank screen and 3DS audio is always silent. Its last check said the headless run was okay for all three consoles, but that check used built-in demo programs and the 3DS demo writes straight into the frame buffer. The second app is the Docker alternative with three out of 10. It wrote a Rust runtime called Dockyard that pulls real images from Docker Hub, imports Docker save files correctly, and builds simple Docker files with caching, but a crafted image layer can write files outside the store through a symlink and that is an automatic cap at three. On macOS, it is also not a container at all. If you run Alpine's shell, you actually get the Mac's own shell running on your real file system and the memory limit is not enforced. The README still claims it is faster than Docker with no measurement. The third app is the Room Designer and this is its best score at 6.6. Changing the room size rebuilds real walls. There are 16 procedural furniture shapes. Dragging and rotating respect the walls and colored lights really tint the scene, but the default view sits under a milky white haze where about 40% of the pixels are near white. And if you reload the page, your design is gone because there is no save, no export, and no undo. That 6.6 is just above Carbon's 6.3 and well below Argon's 8.1. The fourth app is the keyboard configurator with 3.5. This one looks great. The black and yellow UI is strong and consistent. It connects with the correct VI filter and single key changes do land on the keyboard, but it never reads the keyboard. After you connect, you are editing the app's own built-in profile, not your actual keymap. Macros are never sent, even though a toast tells you they were written to EEPROM, and two command IDs are swapped, so a lighting write is really a read. The fifth app is Pokémon Red with three out of 10, and this is the one that hurts because Carbon got 8.2 here and Argon got 8.7. Hydrogen built the Parcel errand, the Old Man, the Forest, and Brock with the badge and prize money, and it runs at a steady 60 frames per second, but Route 1 has a ledge across its full width that only lets you jump south, so you can never walk north to Viridian City, and only six of the 16 maps are reachable on foot. Its final message says the tests cover the full quest from Pallet Town to beating Brock. That test teleports the player between stages, sets the enemy to 1 HP, and forces the win. The last app is the Fitbit desktop app with 5.6, which is above both Carbon at 5.4 and Argon at 5.2. Its strain and training load maths was reproduced correctly on all 49 days, and TCX, JSON, and CSV imports work, but it is built around demo data. Your imports get merged into a seated fake athlete called Alex Mercer. Missing heart rate values are filled in with baseline numbers, and importing the same file twice doubles every workout. The package desktop build also cannot reach its own backend, so the total is 24.9 out of 60, which is 41.5%. That is rank 14 out of 15 models, and only Minimax M3.1 Flash is below it with 21.8. Kinesis 4 Max has 30.6, Carbon has 32, Argon has 32.6, GPT 6.1 Soul has 33, GPT 6 Astra has 33.9, Opus 5.5 has 34.7, and Fable 5.2 still leads with 42. So on artificial analysis, Hydrogen beats Argon by a point, and on my bench it is 7.7 points behind Argon. The upside is cost. All six apps came to $6.04 at list price and 13.1 million tokens, and the whole batch finished in 31 minutes. Carbon cost $23.04 and used 76.5 million tokens, and its lowest app alone took 161 minutes. Now, how it behaves because that explains most of the scores. The first thing is that it barely thinks. Across all six tasks, it used 37,931 reasoning tokens, only 8% of its output. The container runtime is 3,643 lines of rust, and it used 188 reasoning tokens for the whole thing. The second thing is that it writes everything first and compiles later. In the emulator, it wrote 34 files across five crates before its first cargo check at step 23. In Pokémon, it wrote every source file, then the test file, and ran the first test at step 32 of 36. It recovered quickly from every build error it saw, and it never got stuck in a loop. The third thing is that it is completely silent. Every run has exactly one visible message, which is the final summary. You get no plan, no progress updates, and no todo list. The fourth thing is the strangest. In the container task, it spent 31 of 63 steps exploring the Mac. It compiled small Swift programs against Apple's virtualization framework, signed them with entitlements, searched the disk for a Linux kernel, and proved that a VM would work. Then it shipped no VM and no isolation at all. The fifth thing is the real problem. It never looks at what it built. In six runs, it did not view a single screenshot. In Pokémon, it found Chrome at step three and never opened the game. In the room designer, it tried one screenshot. Chrome crashed and or true at the end of the command hid the crash, and it moved on. For the three web apps, verified meant that the server returned a page, and in the container task, its last check printed okay, which it took as success, but that okay came from the Mac's shell, not the container. To be fair, every final message has a limit section, and it is honest about the things it noticed. It said the DS 3D engine is a stub, that the Fitbit login was never tested, and that the screenshot failed. It is wrong only about the things it never checked, but that is most of what matters. So, here is my take. Hydrogen is not a weak model. The Game Boy Color and the Fitbit Maths are correct, and its UIs are the best part of its output. Its weakness is that it decides it is done far too early, and its tests are written to pass on a benchmark where nobody opens the app that does not show. On mine, it shows on every app. I would not give Hydrogen a whole app and walk away. I would give it a narrow task with a clear test that somebody else wrote. And at this price and speed, that is a good deal. This is also how I would use it in Panda Code. Panda Code is my app for running coding agents as a team. An architect plans the work and splits it into assignments. Workers on different models do those assignments, and a router picks the cheapest model that is likely to pass each one. Hydrogen fits the worker slot well. Write this module, fix this build error, add these endpoints. It is fast and cheap, and it does not loop. What it should not do is decide that the job is finished. That decision belongs to the architect on a stronger model and to a reviewer that actually opens the app. A teleporting test like the Pokémon one is exactly what a reviewer catches and what Hydrogen alone ships. Google clearly thinks the same way. Anti-Gravity has a new orchestrator where carbon coordinates and Hydrogen runs the worker and verifier agents. And Google says it gets close to carbon's success rate with 24% less quota. That is Google's number, not mine. And from what I saw, I would use Hydrogen as a worker, but I would not use it as the verifier. Finally, the big question, is Google really behind in the AI race now? My answer is no. Google is not behind overall. It is behind in one lane, which is coding agents that build a whole app alone. And for developers, that is the lane that matters most right now. In that lane, the numbers are clear. On my bench, Google's best model is Argon in fifth place, 9.4 points behind Fable 5.2 and also behind Opus 1.5 and both OpenAI models on artificial analysis. Fable at max effort is five points ahead of Carbon. But look at everything else. Google shipped Argon to developers in mid-October, Carbon at the end of October, and Hydrogen on November 12th. So that is three models in about a month. On the Vales index, the top six models are all Anthropic and Google, and Hydrogen is sixth. Hydrogen went into Google search for all users on day one, and the Gemini app reportedly passed a billion monthly users. And Hydrogen costs a fraction of Fable 5.2, which is $8 and $40. Anthropic needs the best model to win. Google only needs a good enough model in front of everyone at a low price, and it already has that. So in my opinion, Google is not losing this race. It is losing the coding agent race to Anthropic, and the fix for that is a model that checks its own work, not a faster one. Overall, Hydrogen is a fast, cheap worker with a bad sense of when it is finished. Use it under a stronger lead and do not trust it when it says the job is verified. Anyway, [music] let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

items.title: Meta just opensourced a 100-File Skill Library for Better UI Designs!
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll be taking a look at Astryx, the design system Meta grew internally over eight years and has now open-sourced under the MIT license, built so that you and your coding agent use the same system from the same docs. I'll go through what you get, from more than 150 accessible React components and page templates to StyleX without any build setup, CSS-variable themes and the swizzle command. Then I'll show the agent side in a real Vite React app, with init writing the rules into CLAUDE.md, the build command picking a template instead of generating code, the lookup commands, the hosted MCP server and the agent skill. After that, I'll look at Meta's nightly vibe tests against shadcn and raw HTML, including the bad night they published. Finally, I'll cover the downsides and who should actually try it.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Astryx grew inside Meta over the last eight years and powers mo
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So so Meta has open sourced a design system called Asterix, and the pitch is a bit different from what we usually see. It's not just a set of nice-looking React components. It's built so that you and your coding agent use the same system from the same docs in the same way. And this isn't some new side project. Asterix grew inside Meta over the last eight years, and it became the biggest design system in the company. It powers more than 13,000 internal apps. They released it in beta back in June, and it's at about 18,700 stars on GitHub now under the MIT license. Now, the reason I wanted to talk about it is simple. If you ask an agent to build you a UI today, you mostly get the same thing every time. A bunch of divs, random hex colors, some Tailwind classes, and a layout that kind of works but doesn't feel like it belongs to anything. Asterix tries to fix that by giving the agent a real system to build with and a way to look things up instead of guessing. So let's get right into it. First, a quick look at what you actually get. There are more than 150 components according to the README, and the CLI I installed actually lists 174 of them. These are accessible React components with full TypeScript types, so you get things like an app shell, dialogs, tables, forms, date pickers, and all the usual stuff. On top of that, there are page templates and block templates which are full layouts like a dashboard, a login page, a settings page, or an AI chat screen that you can drop straight into your app. It's written with Stylex, but you never have to touch Stylex yourself. You just import two pre-built CSS files and use the components. So there's no build plugin, no PostCSS setup, and no Babel config. And if you want to change how something looks, you pass a clinance, and that can be Tailwind CSS modules or plain CSS, whatever your project already uses. theming works the same way. A theme is just a set of CSS variables, so you can make the whole system look like your own brand without forking or wrapping the components. There are seven themes right now, neutral, butter, chocolate, stone, gothic, and Y2K. And there's dark mode built in. And when you do need full control over a component, there's a command called Swizzle. It copies the full source of that component into your project, so you own it from that point. Kind of like the Shadcn approach, except you only do it for the components you actually want to change, and the rest still get upstream fixes. Now, let's come to the part that I think makes Astro interesting, which is the agent side. Their main idea is that the CLI is the docs. The documentation website actually reads from the CLI, not the other way around. So there's only one copy of the docs, and it can't drift out of sync. They even have a blog post titled The Best CLI is One You Never Run, because the idea is that your agent runs it for you. So let me show you how this works in a real project. I made a fresh Vite React app and installed the Astro core package, the neutral theme, Stylex, and the CLI. One small thing to keep in mind here, before the CLI is installed in your project, plain NPX Astro points to a different unrelated package on NPM. So use the full package name at Astro design/CLI until it's installed. The first command is init. You tell it which agent you use. So Claude, Cursor, Codex, and a few others, and it writes a managed block into that agent's instruction file. For Claude, that's the cloud.md file. This block tells the agent how to build with Astro. Start every page from a template. Don't write raw divs. Don't hard code hex colors or pixel values. Look up a component before using it and run the doctor command when you're done. Then there's the build command, and this one is pretty cool. You describe what you want in plain English, like a settings page for a SaaS app, and it doesn't generate code. Instead, it picks the closest page template, suggests the blocks to fill it with, and lists the components for whatever is left. Meta's reasoning is that AI is a copycat, so they gave it good examples to copy, which honestly makes a lot of sense to me. From there, the template command copies that settings template straight into your project. I added the theme with theme add neutral, wired up about 15 lines in the main file and started the dev server, and this is what you get. A full settings page with a sidebar forms, toggles and proper spacing. And it took a few minutes, most of which was npm install. There are also commands for looking things up. You can search across components, hooks, docs, templates and themes in one ranked list. You can ask for a single component's props and you get the exact types, the variants and the defaults, so the agent doesn't have to invent props that don't exist. And every command can return JSON with stable error codes plus a dense mode that cuts down on tokens. There's even a manifest command that describes the whole CLI, which they call an open API spec for the CLI. And if you don't want to use the CLI at all, there's a hosted MCP server. You add it to Claude code with one command and your agent gets two tools, search and get, which pull from the same docs. There's also an LLMS to EXT file on the site. And if you install the CLI globally and run init user, it writes an asterisk skill into your home folder and links it into Claude code and a few other agents. So every project you open already knows asterisks. Now the other thing I liked is that they actually measure this. In the repo, there's a folder for what they call vibe tests. Every night they give agents the same set of UI prompts and build them four ways, with asterisks, with asterisks plus Tailwind, with Shadcn and Tailwind, and with raw HTML. Then a separate judge agent scores the results. On a good on a good night, Asterisk scored 98, Shadcn scored 95, and raw HTML scored 82. But they also published a bad night where Asterisk dropped to 77 because the agent made up imports and props. And they openly say that Shadcn wins the most nights across their full record. I really respect that because most companies would only show you the good chart. Now let's talk about the downsides because there are a few. It's still in beta and on version 0.7 with new releases almost every day, so expect things to move. It needs React 19 or newer and the CLI needs node 22.13 or newer. So, if your app is still on React 18, this is not for you yet. Only the neutral theme is marked as maintained right now, and every other theme is a separate package you install first. The charts package is only on the Canary channel, and if you swizzle a component, you then need a style X compiler in your build, or that page won't render. Also, the agent rules are pretty strict. No divs and no raw hex values is a great rule for consistency, but if your team lives in Tailwind utility classes, you'll have to decide how much of that you want to follow, and the bundle isn't small either. My single demo page came out at around 600 kilobytes of JavaScript before Gzip. So, should you use it? If you're starting a new React 19 app and you build a lot of UI with agents, I think Asterix is worth trying. The templates, the build command, and the CLI as Doc's idea actually change what the agent produces, and you can feel it on the first page. If you already have a mature app on ShadCN or MUI, I'd wait a bit until it leaves beta and maybe try it on a side project first. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super [music] Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

items.title: Ghostty's creator made an Agent GUI & it's quite good!
items.summary:
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

Superlogical: https://superlogical.com
Mitchell's announcement post: https://mitchellh.com/writing/superlogical
Program status protocol (OSC 7501) write-up: https://mitchellh.com/writing/program-status-osc7501

In this video, I'll walk you through Rex, the new terminal from Superlogical, the company started by Mitchell Hashimoto, the creator of Ghostty. I installed the beta on my Mac, so I'll show you what it is and how it differs from Ghostty, how access, tabs, themes and the Lua config work, and what its rex command line can do.
